extracted.intended_audience: TeX/LaTeX users (mathematicians) typesetting commutative diagrams with XY-pic
extracted.subtask_description: Practical tutorial guidance for constructing commutative diagrams using the XY-pic package (kernel and arrow/frame/curve extensions) in Plain TeX or LaTeX. Covers the basic elements (positions, objects, directionals), arrow construction and labelling, curved and multiple arrows, text in diagrams, and naming/coordinate techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steps to construct a diagram
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus, to construct a diagram with XY-pic, you have to use the following steps: 1. choose the positions (the coordinates) of the vertices of the diagram; 2. drop some objects at these positions (these objects will be the origins and targets of the arrows); 3. connect the positions with arrows; 4. add whatever extra information you want (e.g. labels or text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the four-step workflow as a canonical pipeline for creating diagrams; many later examples illustrate each step in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positions (coordinate system)
rubrics_metrics.description: positions – they are nothing but the pair of coordinates of a point of the figure. The coordinate system is local: it is related to each figure, not to the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose coordinates per-figure; coordinates are local to the xy environment. Use explicit coordinates for flexible spatial placement (the alternative xymatrix uses an array-style placement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects (placing labels/boxes)
rubrics_metrics.description: objects – they are thought of as boxes that, unlike ordinary TEX boxes, have edges. They can be circular, elliptic or rectangular and there is an entire set of operations that can applied to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place objects with operators like *{...} and *+{...} (the + introduces some extra space around labels). Objects are the origins/targets of arrows; consider using framed/shape extensions later for different object shapes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directionals: connectors and tips
rubrics_metrics.description: directionals – they provide ways of connecting different positions and can be of two kinds: 1. connectors – they are used to construct the shaft (the body) of the arrow; 2. tips – they are used to construct the tail and the head of the arrow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connectors use **\dir{...} syntax and link the last two positions; tips require the ? operator (?>* for head near last position, ?<* for tail at origin). Always put a semicolon ; before defining a new position; use + after * to add space so the connector isn't too close to the label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using the ? operator to place tips and intermediate tips
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding a head or a tail (or both) to a line to produce an arrow is slightly more complicated. The syntax for the command producing a tip is identical to the one of the connector, only the argument is of a different kind, e.g. \dir{>}. What we have to do is to use another operator, ?, to indicate, first, where the tip should be added. The full syntax is ?>*, if we want to add the tip at the end (i.e. near last deﬁned position), or ?<* if we want to add the tip at the origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can put tips at intermediate positions with multiple < or > signs (e.g. ?<<<*), or with a fraction ?(.5)* to place at a decimal position along the connector.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite arrows (\ar) and the arrow option
rubrics_metrics.description: To simplify the syntax for directionals, XY-pic also provides “composite” directionals, i.e. arrows. To use them, you have to activate the option arrow. For instance, to draw an arrow from a position to another, we have to use something like \ar@{-} (\ar is a shorthand for \ar@{->}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activate the arrow extension (or use \usepackage[...]{xy} / \xyoption{...}) to use \ar@{type} shortcuts. Table 3 in the document lists common types; further customization is possible via \ar@variant{tail shaft head} or \ar@{head}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrow variants: ^, _, 2, 3 (above/below/double/triple)
rubrics_metrics.description: The four available variants are: ^ – the “above” variant; _ – the “below” variant; 2 – the “double” variant (shaft is doubled); 3 – the “triple” variant (shaft is tripled).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variants change tip/shaft placement or multiplicity. Behavior depends on the tip: ^/_ may place a tip eccentrically ('above' meaning left when looking tail→head). Using 2/3 doubles/triples the shaft, but enlarging tips to match doubled/tripled shafts is generally useless (tips are not enlarged), so be cautious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrow heads and tails (tip shapes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The head and the tail (i.e. the tips) can be any of the combinations from the table 4. In the table they are shown as heads of arrows, but they can be used, equally, as tails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick heads/tails from the provided repertoire (>, <, >>, <<, |, o, etc.) and combine with shaft styles from \dir arguments. Use \ar@variant{tail shaft head} to explicitly specify components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curved arrows (curve option and syntax)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes we have to use curved arrows... It is possible to do that with XY-pic in a very simple manner. Beware, first of all, that the option curve has to be active. The syntax of the command is \ar@{type}@/_length/ or \ar@{type}@/^length/.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use @/_length/ or @/^length/ to curve below/above respectively; any TeX unit is accepted; omitting length uses a default curvature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labelling arrows: direct labels and exponent/index labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting a label on an arrow is not difficult. If you construct the arrow by indicating separately the body and the tips, then you can add a label in the following way: core is ?*{\alpha} with optional shifts like ?*!/_2mm/{\alpha}. If you draw an arrow by using a specific command, then you have two opportunities: ?*!/_2mm/{\alpha} placed after the arrow, or \ar^{\alpha} (exponent style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish label methods: ?*! syntax places a label on/near the arrow with explicit shifts; ^ and _ create exponent/index-style labels (smaller font). Use |{label} to interrupt the arrow and place the label inside the shaft. Use !/_2mm/ or similar to shift the label; use decimals (0..1) or < / > repeats to position label along the arrow; a leading - places the label on the geometrical middle of the arrow when source/destination widths differ. For consistent font sizes when mixing methods, adjust with {\displaystyle ...} or {\scriptstyle ...}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label placement semantics (underscore ^ left/right convention and fractional placement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t get confused: in XY-pic the underscore _ indicates that the label is on the left of the arrow (when looking from tail to head), while the sign ^ indicates that the label should be on the right. By default, labels are on the left. A simpler way of [moving labels] is to use a single decimal number between 0 and 1. 0 is equivalent to < and 1 is equivalent to >, while 0.5 will correspond ... to the middle of the construction (not the middle of the arrow, unless the source and the destination of the arrow have equal width).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use _ / ^ to place labels at ends; use decimal (.4) or fractional position to precisely place label along the construction; remember placement is relative to the object+arrow bounding box, not just the arrow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple labels on one arrow
rubrics_metrics.description: You can put more then one label on the same arrow: {\ar^(0.3){\alpha}_(0.7){\beta} ...}
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ^(position){label} and _(position){label} to place multiple labels; choose positions to avoid overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifting multiple arrows (@<dimension>)
rubrics_metrics.description: To draw several arrows between the same position, all we have to do is to shift them a little bit. This is done with the command @<dimension>. If the arrows have opposite directions, then the shifting can be made with the same (positive) quantity; otherwise one of them should be shifted with a negative quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use @<1.ex> or negative amounts to separate parallel arrows; for opposing arrows shifting both in the same direction produces symmetric separation. Combine with curvature for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming positions for non-sequential references
rubrics_metrics.description: The trick is to give names to different positions and then address them by their names... we assigned to each position a name (don’t forget the quotation marks!), and then we used the names to define arrows from a position to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name positions with "name" syntax and then use \ar "a";"b" to draw arrows non-sequentially — this is essential for complex spatial diagrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creating holes (interruptions) in arrows
rubrics_metrics.description: What we are doing is to insert a hole in one of the arrows, at the “right place”. With the command |>>... (put as many > sign as it takes), you just fix this position. This is done by trial and error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use |>>>>{\hole} with repeated > or a fractional position |(.33){\hole} to place a hole; placement usually requires trial-and-error to align with other arrows/objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding ordinary text inside diagrams (\txt)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary text is added in a diagram through the command \txt<width>style{text string>. The text is typeset in centered paragraph mode, i.e. the line breaks can be controlled through the command \\.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify <width> and style (e.g. a macro for \small\itshape). One or both options can be absent. \txt works outside the xy environment, but is only useful inside since positions are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: XY-pic environment syntax and package/option activation
rubrics_metrics.description: If used by Plain TEX, it is loaded by \input xy. If used in a LATEX document, then it is loaded by \usepackage[options]{xy}. In Plain TEX you can activate an option by the command \xyoption{option}. With a single notable extension, which will be described below (the \txt construction), all XY-pic constructions should be enclosed in an environment, called xy. For this environment, two syntaxes are provided: Plain TEX version: \xy ... \endxy; LATEX version: \begin{xy} ... \end{xy}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In LaTeX you may use either xy environment syntax; activate extensions via \usepackage[options]{xy} or \xyoption in Plain TeX. If unsure, activate option all — but be aware some options are not included in 'all' and need to be specified separately (see reference manual).

rubrics_metrics.name: Everything inside xy environment is in math mode
rubrics_metrics.description: We mention, in the end of this short description, that everything that happens inside an xy environment is in mathematical mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want ordinary text inside a diagram use \txt; to number diagrams include the xy environment inside an equation environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensions vs features (which to activate)
rubrics_metrics.description: the system also includes some extra goodies, which are called options... they are, somehow arbitrary, divided into two classes: 1. extensions – they add some more objects and methods. Typical for this kind of enhancement of the kernel are the extension frame ... and the extension curve; 2. features – they provide notations for particular applications areas. Typical for this class fall the options: arrow, matrix, polygons, lattices, knots, 2cell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enable only the extensions/features you need (arrow for composite arrows, curve for curved arrows, matrix/xymatrix for array-style diagrams, 2cell for 2-cells). Use frame extension for framed objects; the second article covers frame/matrix/2cell in detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolons and operators syntax rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice, also, that we have to add a semicolon ; before any new position is deﬁned. The connector provides a link between the last two positions we defined. Adding a head or a tail (or both) to a line to produce an arrow is slightly more complicated... The core of the label is ?*{\alpha}. If we would use only that, the label would stay on the arrow. The part !/_2mm/ represent a shift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember syntax conventions: end position definitions with ;, use ** for connectors, ? for tips, ?*! for labelled tip placement, and use !/shift/ to move labels. Small syntax errors (missing semicolon, missing *) commonly produce unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing construction methods: font-size and style consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: There is, though, a small problem: the fonts used for the two arrows have different sizes... If you prefer the larger size, just substitute, in the 'inner' label, {\alpha} by {\displaystyle \alpha}; otherwise substitute in the 'outer' label {\alpha} by {\scriptstyle \alpha}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When mixing label methods (exponent-style vs inline) you may need to manually adjust font size/style to keep labels visually consistent; prefer explicit style commands when combining curved and straight arrows or composite/directional constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the xymatrix/matrix extension for array-style diagrams (trade-off)
rubrics_metrics.description: the xymatrix environment (enclosed in the matrix extension), allowing the representation of the diagrams as arrays (matrices) of objects, providing an easier and more straightforward way of constructing diagrams, without using coordinates to identify the position (but, also, losing some of the flexibility);
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For grid-like diagrams prefer xymatrix for convenience; for highly spatial or precisely positioned diagrams use explicit coordinates in the xy kernel for maximal flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical approach and trial-and-error for fine placement
rubrics_metrics.description: We tried to use in a systematic way the 'learning by examples' approach... many placements (holes, label shifts) are done by trial and error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn by experimenting with the examples provided; expect to tweak repeated < or > signs or fractional positions and small shifts to get precise visual alignment.
